q: Why does the Lean Startup method recommend building a very simple version of your product first instead of trying to build a "perfect" product before showing it to customers?
a: It allows you to charge a luxury price later when you release the finished version of the product.
It prevents local tax authorities from classifying your activity as a real business during your first two years.
It lets you get real customer feedback and improve step by step, making you sixty percent more likely to succeed.
It keeps your daily production volume small enough that you never need to keep financial records or track costs.
quote: The core idea is simple: Build a very simple version of your product or service, get customer feedback, and improve it step by step. Research by MIT shows that businesses using this approach are 60% more likely to succeed than those that try to build a 'perfect' product before showing it to customers.
topic: Chapter 4: Lean Startup in a No-Capital Environment
distractor_pool: It allows you to charge a luxury price later when you release the finished version of the product.
It prevents local tax authorities from classifying your activity as a real business during your first two years.
It keeps your daily production volume small enough that you never need to keep financial records or track costs.
It tricks competitors into thinking your business is failing so they ignore your market entry.
It satisfies the mandatory trial period required before you can apply for a municipal business license.
It guarantees that customers will never ask for refunds or complain if the product fails to work.

audit: Chapter 4 (p. 34) explains that the Lean Startup approach builds a simple version first to get customer feedback and improve step by step, which MIT research shows makes businesses 60% more likely to succeed than trying to build a perfect product first; none of the 10 chapters support tax evasion, skipping cost tracking, or paid advertising budgets.

Competitors are legally prohibited from selling similar products within a five-mile radius of your home workshop.
Ideas are worthless without execution, and your local knowledge and customer relationships are worth more than the idea itself.

topic: Chapter 4: Lean Startup in a No-Capital Environment
distractor_pool: Local municipal laws automatically grant a two-year legal monopoly to the first person who tests a new product.
